newsitem.title: UK: Copper is dizzy above $2,000 a tonne.
newsitem.headline: Copper is dizzy above $2,000 a tonne.

text.p: The price of copper lost its nerve on Monday after a sudden rally that extended gains beyond the psychological barrier of $2,000 per tonne.
It hit a high at $2,042 compared with $2,027 on Friday on the London Metal Exchange (LME) but dropped by late afternoon almost to $2,010.
The metal seemed poised to shake off the blues that have prevailed since the disgrace back in June of the Japanese mastermind of a high price copper trading strategy, Yasuo Hamanaka.
Floor traders cited declines on warehouse stocks of copper that have fallen 60 percent from a peak last year to just 145,825 tonnes.

Fresh stocks data on Tuesday may be crucial but speculators sold to take profits during Monday and trade selling also kicked in after the buying spree failed to drive copper above $2,050. Market "bears" still worry that long positions wait to be unwound by banks who took over the massive exposure of Sumitomo Corp of Japan, after it fired Hamanaka and alleged he had run up losses of $2.6 billion in rogue trades. Traders add that there is a question mark over whether copper moving out of LME stocks is being consumed or just shifted to yards in Europe or China.
Aluminium eased with flagship copper.
Elsewhere on the commodity markets, Chicago wheat futures were little changed to easier despite weekend news of big Egyptian imports at around $3.85 per bushel for December.
But oil prices firmed again after talk of trouble at a giant Texas refinery.

Traders in the United States suspected a problem at Amoco's Texas City refinery after the company bought as much as 300,000 barrels of gasoline on the spot market, presumably to cover lost output. Company officials were unavailable for comment

Benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude oil futures traded in London were up more than 25 cents just above $24.50 a barrel. But gold and the other precious metals markets traded very narrow ranges in markets seeking direction after gains from a modest rally eroded last week.
Bullion fixed virtually unchanged in London at $382.90 an ounce although it edged up later.

Coffee firmed but in thin trading volume in mostly technical trade and cocoa futures skidded, as speculators sold off on a belief that there was a big long player in the New York market. Some key commodity prices at 1730 GMT on Monday
